title: What 'must' and 'can' must and can mean
author: Angelika Kratzer
version: 1977, pp. 337-355, collected with the 1981 and 1991 papers in Modals and Conditionals, Oxford University Press, 2012

record.source: The relational account of modality: a modal is not a word with a meaning but a reading fixed by two parameters and a force. Read for the shape of the kind taxonomy, not for modal logic.
record.kept: The two parameters and the force. A modal is read against a modal base, the set of worlds the conversation makes accessible, and an ordering source, the propositions that rank them; its force is universal or existential. Deontic and epistemic are then not primitive flavours of a word but what a base and an ordering source produce.
record.rewritten: Stated as a procedure for one sentence at a time: the base is deontic when the sentence states what a reader owes and epistemic when it states what is the case, the ordering source is the check the sentence answers to when there is one, and the force is necessity, graded or possibility. The five kinds are the cells that procedure yields, which is why `permission` and `claim` are the two existential cells rather than additions to a list.
record.added: The consequence for enforcement, which the framework does not draw. Because the base and the ordering source are context the sentence does not carry, classifying a sentence is a standard applied by a reader and never a gate; that is our inference, and it is what explains the 2026-10-17 agreement result.
record.dropped: The formal semantics: possible-worlds quantification, the notional category distinctions, conditionals, and the arguments with Stalnaker and Lewis. None of them changes how a sentence is classified, and this repository writes no modal logic.
